title: Hurricane Nolo: Slow, Soaking, and Strengthening Toward Hawaii
summary:
Hurricane Nolo is moving so slowly that it's practically parked over the Pacific. On Friday it was churning toward Hawaii at just 5 mph, and forecasters say that slow pace is exactly what makes it dangerous.

People on the Big Island are under a hurricane watch, meaning hurricane conditions could arrive within 24 to 36 hours. Nolo isn't expected to make landfall this weekend, but the National Hurricane Center warns it will bring "life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides." Some areas could get more than 2 feet of rain, with 10 to 25 inches expected more widely.

As of Friday afternoon, Nolo's maximum sustained winds were 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. Over the next 72 hours, those winds could top out at 140 mph — a Category 4 storm. Warm ocean water is fueling its growth.

The storm's path has been unpredictable. Earlier this week, it was heading west across open ocean when it suddenly turned right, aiming north toward the Big Island. Last week, forecasters had actually declared the system was dissipating. Then it regenerated, became Tropical Storm Nolo, and strengthened into a hurricane.

Nolo is the latest in a busy Pacific hurricane season. Warm water is feeding a powerful El Niño, which is sparking storms worldwide. The Pacific has already seen three Category 5 hurricanes: Genevieve, Lowell and Polo.

Hawaii is still recovering from a brutal year. In March, a Kona low caused the worst flooding in over two decades. In May, a 6.0 magnitude earthquake shook the Big Island. In August, Hurricane Lala raked the islands, and earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell pummeled Kauai. Governor Josh Green said these disasters damaged or destroyed about 1,290 homes, with recovery costs estimated at roughly $1 billion before Nolo even arrives.

"The time to finish preparations for significant heavy rain and flooding impacts on the Big Island is now," the NHC said. Hurricane season in Hawaii runs through November 30.
why_it_matters: As warming oceans feed stronger, slower, rain-heavier storms, Nolo shows how one hurricane can land on a community still rebuilding from the last disaster — shaping where families can safely live, what insurance costs, and how governments spend their emergency money.

background_read: Hawaii is a chain of islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, and the Big Island (the largest island in the chain) sits closest to where Nolo is heading. The National Hurricane Center (the U.S. government office that tracks and forecasts tropical storms) rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale, where higher numbers mean stronger winds — Category 4 storms have winds of at least 130 mph.

El Niño (a recurring climate pattern in which unusually warm Pacific water shifts weather worldwide) is one reason this season has been so busy, because warm ocean water works like fuel for hurricanes. Hawaii's hurricane season runs from June through November, but storms rarely make landfall there since the islands are tiny targets in a vast ocean.

Even a storm that misses can be devastating: slow-moving systems dump rain over one place for days, and Hawaii's steep volcanic slopes make flash flooding and mudslides especially likely. Governor Josh Green (the state's governor) has had to manage an unusual run of disasters, from flooding to earthquakes to back-to-back hurricanes.

perspectives.description: They argue the early, repeated warnings are the system working: a hurricane watch gives residents 24 to 36 hours to stock water, clear drains and prepare to evacuate. The NHC's message — that the time to finish preparations is now — is meant to prevent deaths, not to scare people.

perspectives.perspective: Residents of a state already hit four times
perspectives.description: People still repairing homes from the Kona low floods, the earthquake, Hurricane Lala and Hurricane Lowell face another round of boarding up and packing. With recovery costs already near $1 billion, some question how many times a community can absorb a hit before families give up and leave.

They point out that Nolo is not a freak event but part of a pattern: warm water and a strong El Niño produced three Category 5 Pacific hurricanes in one season. Slow-moving storms are especially troubling because they drop all their rain in one place for days instead of sweeping through.

With hurricane season running through November 30, the question is what Hawaii invests in next — better drainage and flood control, clearer evacuation routes, and disaster funds that can handle repeat events rather than one-off emergencies.
